data.title: Enjoy the Windows 10 Update Experience at London's O2
data.description:
BORK!BORK!BORK! Windows 10 is lingering on after its friends have gone home, plaintively flickering out an update notification on a digital sign at London's O2 arena.

The sign was advertising the venue and some of the activities available inside, including an indoor skydiving experience. We'd recommend indoor skydiving as an alternative to jumping out of a perfectly good aircraft for those minded to give it a go, although the sight of Windows 10 making its presence felt is less than ideal when considering undertaking an extreme sport.

Indeed, a device bleating about a restart is not something one wants to think about just before you go inside and rely on the center's tech to safely blast you toward the ceiling using a fan mounted below the floor. Certainly, mid-air acrobatics would take on an entirely new frisson if there was the added danger of Microsoft's finest abruptly turning off the hardware to give itself a jolly good update.

We've all been in that meeting when Windows decides a restart is needed mid-presentation. It's not great, and even less so when you're dressed in a jumpsuit, helmet, and about to venture into a column of air.

Not that this hardware was part of the indoor skydiving activity, of course. The digital sign was showing an advertisement for the company beneath the notification. Rather, it's a very visible reminder of how much Windows 11 still has to do before it stamps its predecessor out of significance. According to Statcounter (not the most reliable source, but in the absence of official data from Microsoft, a useful indicator), Windows 11 currently enjoys a market share of just under 70 percent, while Windows 10 stubbornly hangs on at 30 percent.

Windows 10 left support last year, although the security update lights can be kept burning for a few extra years via Microsoft's Extended Security Updates (ESU) program. In June 2026, Microsoft quietly extended the updates for consumers to 2027. Up to three years are on offer for commercial users. For a fee, of course.

Microsoft's extension and the notification on O2's digital sign suggest Windows 10 isn't going anywhere anytime soon. Then again, considering how well things have gone for Windows 11 since release, perhaps it too would benefit from a blast of air from below to lift it convincingly above its predecessor. ®

data.title: Google engineer unplugged every fiber they could see and – surprise! – took down a chunk of the G-Cloud
data.description:
Google Cloud has revealed the embarrassing reason for a partial outage at its us-central1-b region this week: An engineer unplugged it.

The incident spanned 07:41 to 11:52 PT on September 1, and saw a portion of the G-Cloud region experience “severe network degradation and resource isolation.”

“Traffic flow drop rates for resources hosted in the affected area reached 100% during the peak of the incident, resulting in unreachable virtual machines and elevated packet loss,” states Google’s service health report.

The preliminary root cause on that page explains that Google designs its cloudy datacenters so they have “redundancy across multiple routing devices.”

“The system is designed to be resilient to all single device or fiber-path failures, and most double-or triple-failures do not affect customer traffic. To ensure this, the devices and fiber paths are physically separated in each datacenter, with diverse power sources,” the document explains.

But it’s possible to defeat all that redundancy by pulling out all the cables.

“The immediate technical trigger for this event was the inadvertent physical disconnection of network fiber-optic cables during a routine hardware maintenance procedure,” Google explained.

“A procedural error meant that the physical maintenance action sequentially unplugged 100% of fiber paths across all devices within 13 minutes. The nature of the error, combined with the speed of the action, prevented warnings of incorrect action reaching the engineer before complete disconnection.”

Once the engineer disconnected the routers, VMs in one zone of the us-central1-b region lost contact with the outside world. They could at least chat with each other, but users couldn’t contact their VMs to figure out what was going on.

Once Google noticed the situation, it moved traffic away from the routers that the engineer disconnected. At that point its resilience provisions kicked in as traffic automatically shifted what the company described as “healthy capacity elsewhere in the region.”

While that was going on, technicians “identified the disconnected optical links and physically reseated the fibers. Once the physical links were fully restored, traffic flow rates normalized and the traffic was redirected back to return the capacity to service.”

To summarize: A Google Cloud zone went offline because one of the company’s engineers pulled out all the cables that connected it to the internet. Once someone plugged everything in again, it started working.

The Register understands that outfits like Google create detailed procedures for how to safely maintain their infrastructure, and that technicians should always follow them carefully.

It therefore seems like the engineer who pulled the cables failed to observe one of the most basic rules of tech: RTFM. ®

data.title: Canonical shuttering some of its legacy chat channels
data.description:
Canonical is closing off some of its older tools and communications channels for users, although some may remain – just unofficially.

Back in May, Canonical’s Aaron Prisk announced on Discord that the company was closing the Ubuntu Pastebin at the end of June. Now a comment from a different Aaron, Aaron Rainbolt, says that the IRC channels will follow.

The official Ubuntu chat channels are now on Matrix – there’s an introductory site and under Step 3: Join the Ubuntu space there’s a Matrix link to Ubuntu’s area: you can either type /join #community:ubuntu.com or follow a Matrix link. (Note: the preceding link will only work if you have a Matrix client installed, and your browser can open it.) This isn’t unprecedented: the Linux Mint project did much the same back when Mint 22 came out a couple of years ago.

For the record, the Ubuntu Wiki still lists all the for-now-still-official IRC servers and channels. As The Register reported at the time, they are hosted on Libera Chat, which was set up in 2021 after the widely used Freenode imploded. For the time being, the IRC channels should remain open – but they will no longer be official methods of communicating with the company, and users shouldn’t expect any staff to be present, whether that is to help, or to moderate, or anything else.

This vulture is crossing all available extremities that Canonical doesn’t also see fit to close down the Ubuntu mailing lists, from which he’s extracted a great deal of value and entertainment over the last 22 years — as well as giving a lot of advice and tech support. That was the Reg FOSS desk’s entrance into the FOSS community. Back when Ubuntu started, Debian was famously unwelcoming to newbies, and it was around the time that Red Hat pulled the plug on its original community distro.

If you’ve never encountered a pastebin, you may be one of those lucky folks who rarely need to venture into Linux troubleshooting. This often involves reading long screensful of text. This is pain to read aloud, and novices miss critical details. The idea of a pastebin is that you can just copy-and-paste the text into a website, then send a handy short link instead. The snag is that such reams of verbiage can include condfidential info, and the very newbies that might need help most are least skilled at spotting and censoring that.

The orignal pastebin.ubuntu.com disappeared a while ago. There are plenty of alternatives, from the original Pastebin.com – albeit behind Cloudflare protection, which as we reported last year blocks some legitimate accesses. For something less transient, even including revision tracking, Microsoft offers Github Gists.

This has led to a new field of encrypted pastebins. One is the AGPL3 CloakBin, whose developer emailed us to tell us about it. You can host your own with tools such as PrivateBin, or its progenitor ZeroBin. As we quickly discovered, there are many others:

  • Paaster;

  • PasteCrypt;

  • Paste.sh;

  • and Defuse’s PIEbin.

This, of course, is the real value in having an official one: users not only know where to go, but if they’re already using software from that vendor, they can also have some reassurance that they can trust an official tool. Not that we needed one, this could be seen as another demonstration of the problem predicted by Xkcd 927.

IRC and its pastebin are merely the latest examples of older tech Canonical has been phasing out in recent years. Last year, it officially deprecated its old revision control system, the GNU-endorsed Bazaar. The Breezy fork is still somewhat active, although the site has a worrying number of dead links. ®

data.title: Cloud snail-mail service Docmail enters third day stuck in the outbox
data.description:
UPDATED Docmail, a service used by more than 30,000 UK businesses and public sector organizations, has been offline for several days, prompting concern among users.

Operated by CFH Docmail Ltd, the cloud-based hybrid mail service allows users to send physical letters without running their own print rooms or making trips to the post office. In other words, it handles the printing and postage of business communications.

However, Docmail has been unavailable since the start of business on September 2, according to its status page. It initially warned that the service was "experiencing slower than usual processing times," before saying soon afterward:

"Docmail is currently unavailable while we carry out essential maintenance. Our technical team is working to complete the maintenance and restore full service as quickly as possible. We apologise for any inconvenience caused and will provide a further update once the system is available again." 

Throughout the rest of the day, techies continued to deploy "required updates," and the service remained unavailable as work took place to "ensure the service can be brought back online safely and reliably."

A further update on September 3 said Docmail was still "temporarily unavailable while our teams continue to work to restore the service." The company thanked customers for their patience and apologized for the "disruption." At the end of the day, it admitted: "We do not yet have a confirmed restoration time. Work remains ongoing as a priority."

By Friday – day three of disruption – the service remained unavailable, with techies still toiling to restore it and promising further updates when more information became available.

Our attention was drawn to the Docmail debacle by Reg readers concerned about the length of the outage and the lack of a restoration time.

We contacted CFH Docmail for details of the disruption's cause and when it expects the service to be restored.

CFH says many of its more than 30,000 business and public sector customers operate in UK healthcare. It claims that more than 75 percent of medical practices use Docmail for bulk mail and individual patient mailings, such as appointment reminders.

Customers also include NHS Trusts such as Croydon Health Services, while dental practices, pharmacies, opticians, and medical research networks also rely on the service, as do some local authorities and businesses.

While the service remains offline, important communications such as health appointment reminders and letters from local councils may go unsent. ®

Updated at 12.59 UTC on September 4, 2026, to add:

Following publication of this article, a spokesperson at CFH Docmail Ltd, told us: 

"We have been made aware of an issue impacting an isolated server, used by only one client. Out of an abundance of caution and in line with our security protocols we took the decision to take Docmail offline. This proactive step is why the system has been temporarily unavailable.

"Our internal team has been working closely to investigate what happened and to ensure that when all systems are switched back on, it will be entirely safe to do so.

"This process does take time, and we are acting on the advice of external consultants to ensure we are taking the right precautions. While Docmail is ready to be reinstated, we are waiting completion of the external review before doing so. We apologise for the disruption this has caused to our customers and are working to restore service in the quickest but safest way possible."

data.title: Best eSIM for travel 2026: which one offers the best value for money?
data.description:
Comparing travel eSIM prices is not as simple as looking at a provider's homepage. Most companies advertise low starting prices, but what travelers actually pay depends on whether they can buy a plan that matches the length of their trip.

If a provider only offers fixed duration packages, travelers may end up paying for several days of mobile data they do not need. For frequent travelers or longer trips, those extra days can quickly add to the total cost.

The Travel eSIM Value Index 2026 compared three leading travel eSIM providers: Holafly, Saily and Airalo. The ranking looks at five factors that can affect the value of an eSIM before, during and after a trip.

Best value eSIM 2026: Overall results

To determine the best eSIM for travel in 2026, the analysis compared Holafly, Saily and Airalo across five areas: Pricing Efficiency (35 percent), Included Benefits (25 percent), Customer Experience (15 percent), Travel Flexibility (15 percent) and Connection Readiness (10 percent).

Holafly achieved the highest overall score at 91.1/100, ahead of Saily (86.7) and Airalo (78.6). The results show that network quality has become largely comparable across leading providers, meaning the important differences now come from real trip costs, included features, customer experience and flexibility.

Which travel eSIM offers the best value for money?

Price is often the first thing travelers compare, but the cheapest advertised plan is not always the cheapest option for the trip they are actually taking.

Pricing Efficiency accounts for 35 percent of the overall score, making it the most heavily weighted category in the index. Instead of comparing headline prices, the analysis calculates the real trip cost for journeys lasting between 1 and 30 days, based on the plans available from each provider.

Because fixed duration plans can make travelers pay for more days than they need, a plan may look cheaper at first, but the final cost can be higher once you account for the days that go unused.


Airalo and Saily require travelers to buy a 15 day plan for an 11 day trip. That means paying for four days of mobile service they do not need. By contrast, Holafly lets travelers buy exactly the number of days they need, eliminating unnecessary spending.

The same pattern appeared across the trip durations analyzed between 1 and 30 days. By reflecting consistently lower real trip costs across the benchmark, Holafly achieved the highest Pricing Efficiency score at 100/100, while Saily scored 96.3 and Airalo 91.6. This was calculated by giving a 100 to the cheapest overall provider, while competitors lose points based on the exact percentage their plans cost extra. For instance, because Airalo's median costs were 8.4 percent higher than the baseline, its final score was reduced to 91.6.

Paying only for the days you actually use can help keep travel costs down, but your experience abroad also depends on the extra tools that your plan has to offer.

Which travel eSIM includes the most features?

Price is only one part of the best value for money eSIM equation; features matter too, especially when they are included in the plan. Many travel eSIM providers advertise similar prices and unlimited data, but the experience can differ depending on what else comes with the plan at no extra cost.

The benefits category compared eight features commonly used by international travelers, including hotspot sharing, regional and global plans, top ups, security tools and emergency internet access. Providers received higher scores when these features were included as standard rather than charging extra.

Both Holafly and Saily achieved the maximum score of 100, but they offer different features. Holafly is the only provider to include Always On, which gives travelers complimentary backup data if they lose access to their main plan. Saily includes an integrated VPN, while Airalo scored 83.3 because fewer features are included as standard.

These features can make a difference during a trip, but when plans change or something goes wrong, the support and policies behind the purchase matter too.

Which travel eSIM offers the best customer experience?

The experience of using a travel eSIM doesn't end after checkout: when travel plans change or problems arise during a trip, customer support and post-purchase policies can make a significant difference.

To evaluate how efficiently each provider responds in these scenarios, the Customer Experience category combines verified Trustpilot ratings with the refund policy offered by each provider.

While Holafly and Saily share the same Trustpilot rating of 4.7/5, their refund policies are very different: Holafly offers eligible customers up to 180 days to request a refund, compared with 30 days for Saily and 14 days for Airalo.

This combination of customer satisfaction and a longer refund window gave Holafly the highest Customer Experience score at 90.75, ahead of Saily at 69.95 and Airalo at 54.45.

If your trip gets cancelled, generous refund terms protect you. But in a normal scenario, another advantage relies on how easily a plan fits your actual schedule.

Which travel eSIM gives travelers the most flexibility?

Travelers plan their trips differently: some know exactly how long they will be away and want to pay only for those days, while others may extend their stay and need more mobile data once they are already abroad. That makes flexibility an important part of the overall value of a travel eSIM.

To evaluate this, the Travel Flexibility category looked at two factors: whether travelers can buy a plan that matches the exact length of their trip, and whether they can extend an active plan without purchasing a new eSIM.

Providers here take two different approaches to flexibility. Holafly lets travelers customise their plan from 1 to 90 days, ensuring they pay only for the exact duration of their trip, while Saily and Airalo sell plans in fixed blocks but allow users to extend an active plan without buying a new eSIM.

As a result, all three providers achieved a score of 50 in this category, each offering flexibility at a different stage of the customer journey. Holafly offers the best value eSIM before the trip begins, while Saily and Airalo offer it once the trip is already underway.

With all these options and commercial terms varying significantly across brands, travelers might question whether the underlying mobile service itself differs just as much.

Is there really any difference in network quality?

Network quality is often one of the first things travelers look for when comparing providers. Fast activation, reliable coverage and access to 5G networks all matter. However, the differences between leading providers are much smaller than many travelers expect.

For this Connection Readiness category, the Index compares destination coverage, activation speed, multi-network support and 5G availability.

The benchmark found no meaningful difference between the three providers in this category. All achieved the maximum score, reflecting comparable destination coverage, instant activation, multi-network support and 5G availability.

This finding suggests that network quality is no longer the main differentiator among leading travel eSIM providers; the biggest differences come from real trip costs, included features, customer experience and travel flexibility, which account for 90 percent of the overall ranking.

So, which travel eSIM is the most convenient?

Choosing a travel eSIM involves more than finding the lowest advertised price: as leading providers offer similar access to mobile networks, the differences that matter most are how much you actually pay, what is included in your plan and how you are supported if something goes wrong.

The Travel eSIM Value Index 2026 evaluated the five areas that influence that experience: Pricing Efficiency, Included Benefits, Customer Experience, Travel Flexibility and Connection Readiness. Together, they show how much travelers actually pay and how well a provider adapts to different trips.

Based on the combined results, Holafly achieved the highest overall score, positioning it as the best value for money eSIM in 2026 with 91.1/100, followed by Saily at 86.7 and Airalo at 78.6. Holafly ranked first thanks to its combination of the lowest real-trip cost, included features, highest Customer Experience score, and flexible trip durations.

The best travel eSIM is not necessarily the one with the lowest advertised price on a website. It is the one that lets you pay for the days you need, gives you useful features as part of the plan and offers support when you need it.

Content provided by Holafly - Travel eSIM Value Index 2026

data.title: Hugging Face is too important to fall into Nvidia's hands
data.description:
OPINION Nvidia on Thursday announced an agreement to acquire open source AI evangelist and model depot Hugging Face for $12.9 billion in a deal that's expected to close next year, assuming regulators don't get in the way.

They should get in the way.

As antitrust magnets go, Nvidia buying Hugging Face takes the cake. You wouldn't let an automaker acquire the primary means of fuel distribution. Nor would you let it buy the primary means by which the mechanics are trained. Yet, Nvidia's acquisition of Hugging Face is tantamount to both.

Unfortunately, the Trump administration likely lacks both the competence and teeth necessary to litigate the case, something that probably factored into CEO Jensen Huang's decision to buy Hugging Face now.

To understand why Nvidia's latest acquisition is so troublesome, we need to talk about just how important Hugging Face has become to the broader AI ecosystem. Have you seen the XKCD comic in which a piece of open source software maintained by a single developer is holding up all of modern infrastructure? It could be argued that Hugging Face is that piece for the AI industry.

Founded in 2016, the AI model repository has become the beating heart of the machine learning community. When a new open weights model drops, Hugging Face is the first place people look. A key element of its success has been its unrelenting commitment to open source AI, which has made it a sort of Switzerland for researchers, enthusiasts, and software devs to collaborate on neutral ground.

If you've ever downloaded an open weights model, it almost certainly came from Hugging Face, whether you knew it or not.

No matter how fervently Nvidia promises not to pollute Hugging Face's hallowed ground, the temptation to use the platform to advance its hardware and software interests will inevitably prove too great for Huang and his lieutenants to resist for long.

In spite of this, Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue sang Nvidia's praises on Thursday, casting the acquisition and the capital it will bring as an opportunity to grow the company's user base from around 18 million today to more than 100 million in the years to come.

Yet, just a year ago Hugging Face rebuffed a $500 million investment by Nvidia, suggesting Delangue knows he's just made a deal with the devil. That said, with a cool $1 billion earmarked for Hugging Face employees joining Nvidia, Delangue and his cohort are going to have plenty of Benjamins with which to wipe away any tears of regret.

What does buying Hugging Face actually get Nvidia?

Nvidia would probably prefer to paint the acquisition as an altruistic move to provide financial security to one of the most important AI resources on the internet today.

The case certainly can be made that Hugging Face is that one brick holding up the rest of the AI ecosystem. If it ever did exhaust its runway, the consequences would be catastrophic.

And Hugging Face's business is capital-intensive. Storing petabytes' worth of AI models and datasets isn't cheap, nor is the bandwidth required to continuously serve those models at scale. Nvidia's involvement all but ensures Hugging Face never has to worry about infrastructure demand going forward.

But while the benefits of Nvidia's patronage are obvious, so is the potential harm to the GPU giant's competitors.

Despite frequent comparisons to GitHub, Hugging Face is more than a place for storing and sharing model weights and training data.

For example, Hugging Face is home to arguably the most comprehensive documentation on AI development on the internet. It wouldn't be hard for Nvidia to use its newfound position to ensure its products are always better documented than its competitors'. You can claim until your face is red that the platform is still "open," but just because something is open doesn't mean it's unbiased.

Then there are Hugging Face's considerable software contributions. If you weren't aware, the popular local AI inference engine llama.cpp became part of Hugging Face earlier this year. Meanwhile, Hugging Face's Transformers Python library — not to be confused with the model architecture — is a key piece of major inference platforms like vLLM and SGLang, which compete directly with Nvidia's own TRT-LLM offering.

The acquisition puts Nvidia in a prime position to prioritize its own hardware and software products. The AI arms dealer wouldn't necessarily need to do something as brash as ending support for competing platforms. It could simply ensure that the models and frameworks it favors are always better documented, and run first on its kit.

One method to tip the scales would be to flood Hugging Face with cheap Nvidia-based compute. Hugging Face has offered compute resources in the form of its inference endpoints, providers, and Spaces for several years now. To supply this compute, Hugging Face worked with numerous providers across a range of hardware, including major cloud providers, inference-as-a-service vendors, and chip designers such as Nvidia, AMD, Cerebras, SambaNova, and Groq.

As Hugging Face's parent company, Nvidia would be in the position to subsidize compute through its various partners and economically incentivize developers to build for its hardware first. The GPU slinger would have to be subtle. Tying a certain percentage of a neocloud's compute allocations to low-cost educational and development resources would be one way to do it without raising too many suspicions.

No matter how you slice it, nor how much Nvidia insists it's totally not going to thumb the scales, its acquisition of Hugging Face has a high likelihood of harming competition. Hugging Face works better as AI Switzerland than it does as part of the most powerful company in the industry. ®

data.title: Prolific Microsoft 0-day hunter drops CrowdStrike Falcon exploit PoC
data.description:
The disgruntled security researcher known as Nightmare Eclipse (aka Chaotic Eclipse, Infinite Nightmare, and now also MSNightmare) is moving away from their singular Microsoft vendetta and on to other vendors. On Thursday, they dropped a new zero-day bug called FalconFlank that affects CrowdStrike’s Falcon endpoint security platform - albeit with a Windows link.

According to the prolific zero-day hunter, FalconFlank is a privilege escalation vulnerability that abuses the Microsoft Office malicious macros remediation feature in CrowdStrike Falcon. This is an automated security tool built into the platform that inspects Microsoft Office documents. If it finds any potentially harmful macros, the feature strips the suspect code and - hopefully - prevents malicious code or other dangerous payloads from executing when users open the document.

“We are actively investigating these claims and advise customers to disable the Microsoft Office File Suspicious Macro Removal Windows policy setting,” a CrowdStrike spokesperson told The Register. “Customers remain protected through the Cloud Anti-malware for Microsoft Office Files settings. We refer customers to the FalconFlank Tech Alert in the CrowdStrike support portal.”

The proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit works on fully updated Windows 11 25H2 and Windows Server 2025 systems running CrowdStrike Falcon with Phase 3 - Optimal Protection as well as the malicious macro removal feature enabled, Nightmare Eclipse said in a GitHub README. “Obviously by the time I drop this Crowdstrike would already have detections for it so if you want to test you either have to add it to the exclusions or obfuscate the PoC and change the dll load technique,” they wrote.

Security sleuth Kevin Beaumont confirmed this exploit works, along with several others Nightmare released over the past week. Beaumont told us that he’s not surprised to see Nightmare digging into other, non-Microsoft zero-days.

“Kinda makes sense they’d branch out to other vendors as there’s problems across the endpoint security space with the quality of the security products in terms of…security unfortunately,” Beaumont told The Register. “Hopefully it causes cybersecurity vendors to up their game, stop hyping hypothetical AI attacks, and instead make their own products secure for customers.” 

FalconFlank follows other vulnerabilities in various endpoint and antivirus products that Nightmare has found and published in the last several days. These include HardBreacher, an elevation of privileges bug in Kaspersky’s endpoint antivirus product. 

“So the problem is now leaking outside of Microsoft,” Nightmare said when they published the HardBreacher PoC last week. “There was poll held against either finding a bug in the home or commercial version and the poll results were the commercial version. At the time of writing this, the proof of concept works in a fully patched windows 11 25H2 & Kaspersky for Endpoint v14.0.0.504.”

Beaumont confirmed that Nightmare’s HardBreacher exploit code works, as does a PoC for an elevation of privileges vuln in Gen Digital’s Avast antivirus software. This zero-day, named PrettyPrague, “will dump the SAM database by abusing a vulnerability in Avast Sandbox and spawn a full SYSTEM shell,” according to the researcher.

"Gen was recently made aware of a security vulnerability affecting a subset of Gen products, including Avast Antivirus, that could allow an attacker to elevate their system privileges," Gen Digital told The Register.

"We immediately initiated our security response procedures and are actively developing a patch. We take all security matters seriously and are committed to addressing this issue swiftly."

Kaspersky did not immediately respond to The Register’s requests for comment.  

Nightmare also recently released an Nvidia memory corruption zero-day vulnerability dubbed GreenSection, but according to Beaumont, this one just crashes the system. Nvidia did not respond to our inquiries.®

data.title: Terminated employee cost company hundreds of thousands because nobody revoked access
data.description:
PWNED Welcome back to PWNED, where we talk about organizations that are independently self-owned. This week’s tale of toxic tech involves a disgruntled ex-employee who had the means and opportunity to wreak havoc.

Our story comes courtesy of Yad Senapathy, who serves as CEO of the Project Management Training Institute in Dallas, Texas. He recalls a time many years ago when he used to work in IT at a company with more than 1,000 employees.

While Senapathy was working there, the company terminated an employee, but nobody cut off his access to internal systems. The angry worker logged back in, then deleted files, locked out other people's accounts, and even corrupted a database. 

"Several days passed where the person was no longer on payroll, but their credentials were still active," Senapathy said. "Nobody had been clearly assigned to shut them off. HR thought IT would handle it once the termination was processed. IT was waiting for HR to send a formal request. I've learned that when nobody is clearly responsible and there is no set deadline, these things can easily get missed until there is already a problem."

This lapse in responsibility meant the terminated employee had access to shared admin credentials, account controls, and project tracking systems. Each of these, in turn, granted permission to other systems, leading to a domino effect of inappropriate access, which the former worker used to wreak revenge on the whole organization. 

According to Senapathy, the damage amounted to hundreds of thousands of dollars. Just as bad were the weeks of delay added to an important project.

As an added irony, recovery was particularly difficult because the systems were damaged by the very person who best knew how to repair them.

“The employee wasn't some genius hacker. They just still had access after they left and nobody changed the credentials or reviewed admin rights,” Senapathy told The Register. “We'd let one person collect so much system knowledge that shutting the door behind them took longer than it should have.”

Senapathy recommends that offboarding checklists and access reviews should be right next to “return the laptop” on that list. The problem in this case is that the terminated employee had more access than most people, and so IT didn't know what they needed to cut off.

“Sadly, it could've been prevented by same-day deletion of access, forced re-review of shared account access and zero tolerance for one person owning a whole system alone,” he said.

This writer can identify with this situation. At a previous job, after I quit, I lost email, chat, and shared drive access, but months later my former boss asked if I could still log into an important database that was hosted externally and show him how to use it. I had no problems getting in.

Have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com. Anonymity is available upon request.®

data.title: Microsoft to bounce mail from outdated Exchange servers
data.description:
Microsoft is upping the ante on Exchange Server security, warning that outdated on-premises systems will soon be blocked from sending email to Exchange Online.

From the second week of September, Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 machines that send email to Exchange Online through an inbound connector of the OnPremises type must be patched to the final public update baseline released in October 2025, according to Microsoft.

"This update level was released almost a year ago," Microsoft stated, "and all organizations should have updated to it."

Microsoft has been advancing its "oldest acceptable version" for some time, but this change takes the baseline to the final public update for Exchange 2016 and 2019. Any subsequent increase would leave only customers enrolled in the Extended Security Update (ESU) program or those who have migrated to Exchange Server Subscription Edition able to meet it.

Organizations may retain on-premises Exchange servers to support hybrid deployments, applications, or other systems that depend on them for email.

According to Microsoft, throttling and blocking apply only to servers sending email to Exchange Online through an inbound OnPremises connector. Other delivery methods are unaffected, and the policy does not necessarily cover "all servers in your organization."

The company added: "This might change in the future," which doesn't sound sinister at all.

Administrators must balance the need to apply security patches promptly against the risk that an update introduces problems of its own – something Microsoft has, to put it delicately, caused in the past. 

Some administrators responding to the announcement were more than a little perturbed, although Microsoft has applied throttling and blocking to "significantly out of date" Exchange Server installations for several years.

The announcement gives administrators advance notice of a change Microsoft says would have happened anyway. "With or without this announcement, the change would have been made (just as it was made in the past, without any announcement)," explained Microsoft Principal Project Manager Nino Bilic.

"The bottom line is that admins really need to understand that updating Exchange should be done on time." ®

data.title: PostgreSQL 19 connects the dots with standardized graph queries
data.description:
PostgreSQL 19 is set to add standardized SQL syntax for querying property graphs.

The open source database has steadily grown in popularity over the last five years, becoming the most popular among developers for the first time in 2023.

Speaking to The Register, Alastair Turner, PostgreSQL evangelist at open source consultancy Percona, said the property graph query support in PostgreSQL 19 – due later this month or early October – resulted from collaboration among several of the database's largest contributors.

Graph databases store data as nodes, relationships, and properties rather than tables or documents. They have advantages for certain workloads, but adopting one can mean adding another DBMS to the technology stack.

The relational database has been acquiring graph query capabilities for some time, but PostgreSQL 19 is set to go further, Turner explained. "All the rest of it has sort of been done through Object Relational Mapping over the top. This is actually baked-in graph syntax. It comes from the SQL 2023 standard."

Turner said the implementation was "very heavily influenced" by some of the engineers behind OpenCypher, the open source query language for graph databases. The work also involved PostgreSQL committers who sit on the SQL standards committee.

"This is one of the most interesting developments because it's one of the big multi-vendor collaborations. There was lots of coding and review work across quite a few of the big contributors," he said.

The new capability implements SQL/PGQ, which became part of the SQL standard in 2023.

"It's on the right path," Turner said. "The SQL community and the PostgreSQL community are going to try to optimize everything."

However, he added that the implementation "still needs one or two additional syntax features" before it can displace dedicated graph databases for a significant number of workloads.

Turner said: "The current implementation creates queries across node-edge graphs to satisfy those requests. So some of them perform very well. What's going to have to happen in the next iteration or two is that indexing add-ons catch up to improve the performance." ®
